sets.transcript: Good morning. Today I'd like to look at why some cities are introducing congestion charges, where drivers pay a fee to enter the city centre at busy times. The main aim is to reduce traffic, but there are other benefits. In London, for example, traffic in the charging zone fell by around thirty percent in the first years, and buses became faster and more reliable. The money raised is usually invested in public transport. Critics argue that the charge is unfair to people on low incomes who have to drive to work, and some businesses worried that fewer customers would visit. Overall, though, most studies suggest that well-designed schemes reduce congestion and pollution without harming the local economy.

sets.transcript: In this talk I'll explain the idea of a growth mindset. Psychologists have found that students who believe their intelligence can develop through effort tend to persist longer when tasks are difficult. In contrast, students who see ability as fixed may avoid challenges because failure seems to prove they are not clever. Interestingly, the way teachers give feedback matters. Praising effort and strategy, rather than saying a student is smart, encourages a growth mindset. However, recent research suggests the effects are smaller than first claimed, and mindset programmes work best when combined with real support, such as good teaching and time to practise.

sets.transcript: Let's talk about food waste. In many wealthy countries, around a third of all food produced is never eaten. Some is lost on farms and during transport, but a large share is thrown away by households, often because people buy too much or misunderstand date labels. 'Best before' dates are about quality, not safety, so food is usually fine to eat after them. Supermarkets are starting to sell imperfect fruit and vegetables at lower prices, and some cities collect food scraps for compost. Reducing waste saves money for families and also cuts greenhouse gas emissions, because rotting food in landfill releases methane.

sets.transcript: Today I want to discuss the history of the bicycle. The first designs in the early nineteenth century had no pedals; riders pushed along the ground with their feet. Pedals were added later, but early models had a huge front wheel, which made them fast but dangerous. The so-called safety bicycle of the 1880s, with two equal wheels and a chain, made cycling popular with ordinary people, including women, and changed the way people travelled to work. Today, bicycles are again seen as a solution to traffic and pollution in cities.
